synopsis: Monte Carlo estimates miss rates by repeatedly drawing scenario parameters from probability distributions and counting outcomes; the booklet recommends it as the honest default for rate estimation and uses a frozen sample for its estimation campaign [f14181, f14182, f14188, f14183]. For large simulation sweeps, it selects the point-mass transient braking model and recommends preparing the Monte Carlo engine, parameter database, metrics and traceability before prototype testing [f6435, f6404]. However, pure Monte Carlo is extremely inefficient for rare dangerous events: a true miss rate of one in 10,000 yields about one miss per 10,000 runs, requiring tens of thousands of runs for a precise estimate, and naive Monte Carlo cannot reach low failure rates within four months [f6834, f14185, f10337]. Precedents include ACAS X validation representing billions of flight hours and a 2005 Griffith University study combining Monte Carlo with a Doppler-radar field demonstration that reported light-vehicle detection at 75 m [f1908, f6368]. For planning, Monte Carlo samples task durations and should communicate milestone uncertainty through P50/P80 S-curves or fan charts; reference class forecasting outperformed Monte Carlo and earned-value forecasting in a 2016 test only when reference-class similarity was high [f16335, f9889, f9606].
